lesson: A git worktree lives inside the main repo at .claude/worktrees/<name>. If its .git file goes missing (pruned or deleted while a session is still running) every git command from that directory silently resolves to the main clone and reports success while driving the wrong repo. Run `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` before any state-changing git command, and prefer `git -C <path>` over relying on the shell's working directory. Caught three sessions, Merger's own included.

Two independent clones of this repo sit on disk, labs/robinhood and labs/crow-archer, with separate refs and separately-stale masters. A branch you cannot find is probably in the other clone. Fetch and fast-forward the specific clone you mean before cutting a branch from its master.

A clean auto-merge with a fully green suite can still drop content. In round 3 it lost 154 lines of docs/architecture.md and docs/manual.md with no conflict, because no test reads prose. After any merge, diff the result against each source branch and read what was not taken, do not trust green plus no-conflict.

Ancestry lies here three ways: squash merges, dropped content whose merge-base became the source tip, and cherry-picks that change the hash. So `N commits ahead` is never proof a branch is unmerged. Verify by content: `git diff --stat origin/master <branch>` read for ADDED lines, or compare `git rev-parse <branch>^{tree}` against master's tree hash.

`git branch -d` refuses a squash-merged branch as `not fully merged` even when every line of it is already on master. That refusal is not evidence of unmerged work. Confirm the branch is contained by content first, then delete with `-D`.

Two sessions can fix the same thing two different ways. Round 4 had it twice: the archer-pierce flake, and a balance-doc drift test written once standalone and once inline. Read the ledger before starting; if your task is already someone's row, say so instead of duplicating the work.

The in-app Browser pane starves requestAnimationFrame while document.visibilityState still reads 'visible', freezing the game clock from page load. This is what the abandoned `freeze at iteration 51` synthetic repro was actually measuring, not a game bug. Drive the loop with `setInterval(() => __game.frame(16.7), 16)` (setInterval still fires, and frame() keeps liveLoop true unlike takeClock()), or verify in a real browser tab.

The crow king's bats ride in the crows array with no `path` field until the scheduler serves them. A tile turning solid in that 1-2 frame window ran invalidateThrough over the whole roster and read `.length` off undefined, throwing inside the rAF callback and freezing the game mid boss fight. Fix: treat a missing path as routeless (`== null`, not `=== null`) and mark `path` optional on PathAgent. A roster that mixes walkers with never-pathing agents must not let one field-less member take the frame loop down.

keyDownAs[e.code] held one name per physical key. Holding a key across a Shift press makes the OS auto-repeat it under its shifted name (w becomes W), orphaning the first entry so keyup clears the wrong one and the key jams its own movement axis. Arrow keys are immune because their name does not shift. Fix: keep the down/up bookkeeping in pure noteKeyDown/noteKeyUp in src/sim/input.ts and release a code's old name when it repeats under a new one.

An intermittent freeze that no synthetic step-loop could reproduce fell in one monitored play session. The instrument: a one-second heartbeat POSTing game vitals plus the drained diagnostic log to a dev-server JSONL sink, with watchdogs that classify the stop (loop-dead, logic-freeze, no-frames, or a hard hang detected by the beat gap from outside). Reach for real monitored play with an out-of-page log sink before trusting a headless repro of a timing bug.

A doubled backslash inside a quoted heredoc collapses before Python sees it, so a match pattern written as \\n arrives as a REAL newline and a multi-line str.replace() pattern built to match source text containing \n scores zero hits. Cost two failed edits in one session, including one spent adding CRLF handling on the theory that line endings were the cause -- the file was LF and the pattern itself was wrong. Anchor a scripted edit on a backslash-free substring, or build the character with chr(92); diagnose a mystery zero-match by printing repr() of each pattern line against the file's real text before blaming line endings. The assert-the-match-count rule is the only reason this failed loudly instead of shipping a no-op edit.

Two branches each added a row to the same JS object literal (the talent STATS table) under the same key. The merge was CLEAN -- the hunks did not overlap -- and produced an object with two longThrow keys, where the language silently keeps the last one and the archer's meaning of the stat won over the wizard's. No test caught it because both keys are valid syntax and the type is an index signature. Reading a merged TABLE row by row is a separate step from reading a merged DIFF: after any merge that touches a shared table, list its keys and assert they are unique.

game.test.ts is CRLF, but a block appended with a Bash heredoc arrives LF, so one file ends up with both. A scripted edit that joins its pattern with CRLF then matches nothing in the LF region and vice versa, and the assert-the-match-count rule fires on a pattern that is character-for-character correct. Cost three failed edits before the cause was visible. Fix: have the edit try both endings (replace chr(10) with CRLF in the pattern and retry), or work per line with splitlines(keepends=True) so each line keeps its own ending. Diagnose by printing repr() of the region rather than reading it, since both endings look identical in any viewer.

Four new tests passed with -t and failed in the full run, from two causes that both look like flakiness and are neither. First: assigning player.aimAngle does not aim. updatePlayer copies it from the pointer on every step, so the aim is whatever the PREVIOUS test left the mouse at -- aim with the arena-testkit aimAt helper and step a frame before firing. Second: crow speed and aggression climb with the run's escalation clock, which earlier tests have already advanced, so a crow that sits still in isolation outruns the thing being measured in a suite. Park a test's target by setting heldTimer, the same hold the ranger's net applies, or assert on terrain, which does not move or get replaced. A count of enemies is also the wrong assertion while waves are spawning: compare by identity.

A pass over the fourteen lessons in this file asked of each one: is there anything that would catch it, or does it rely on someone having read this? Three were mechanisable and none of the three had a guard. merged-table-duplicate-key is now caught by a uniqueness check over every talent and rite id in src/sim/talents.test.ts -- the language refuses two keys in one object literal but has nothing to say about two ARRAY entries sharing an id, which is why the clean merge went through. mixed-line-endings-in-one-file is now caught by src/line-endings.test.ts, which rejects a file at war with itself in either direction rather than mandating an ending. Half of green-alone-red-in-suite is pinned as a characterisation test in game.test.ts: assigning player.aimAngle does not aim, because updatePlayer copies the angle from the pointer every frame. The other eleven are about git, worktrees, clones and the harness, where the cost is real and a test is not the instrument. Worth repeating when this file grows: a lesson nobody has turned into a guard is a lesson the next session pays for again.

Third time this repo has shipped code that quietly skips soldiers. The arrow-vs-body loops handle crows, skeletons and soldiers in three copies, and only the first two routed through spendArrowPierce -- the soldier loop spliced the arrow itself. So everything hanging off that shared call silently did not happen against the garrison: an ultimate sold as piercing without limit stopped dead on the first soldier, and a harpoon meant to reel the hero in never reeled off one. damageEnemiesInRadius carries a comment about the exact same omission from an earlier release. The fix that stops a fourth: one walk over the three lists (forEachHostile), so a new hit SHAPE cannot enumerate two of them and forget the third. When adding anything that hits bodies, grep for the three lists together and make sure you are not writing a fourth enumeration.

A test fired a projectile 300 px at a boss and asserted the effect of the hit. It failed two runs in five, and pinning the boss's position and shield every frame did not fix it -- the shield comes back mid-flight, the bolt is absorbed, and absorbing is not hitting. The cure was not more pinning but a SHORTER window: fire from 90 px so the shot lands within five frames, inside which the entity's state machine cannot turn over. It also failed ALONE and passed in the suite, which is the usual order-dependence inverted and a sign the cause is timing rather than leaked state. When a test must race a live entity, shorten the race rather than freezing more of the world.

Deleting one gameplay rule turned 4 test failures into 376. The rule was a filter -- a talent counted only if the run had drafted it -- and its implementation returned the base BEFORE doing the tree lookup. The lookup throws on an id from another hero's tree, and the generic caller asks by name for talents belonging to whoever is not playing. So the filter had been silently absorbing a throw nobody knew was possible, and removing it uncovered the real defect underneath rather than causing one. The shape to watch for: an early return that answers before the dangerous call is a guard whether or not anyone wrote it as one. Before deleting a rule, look at what its short-circuit skips, not only at what it decides -- and when a deletion produces failures by the hundred, read one of them properly instead of reverting: they were all one missing guard, restored in three lines.

Three tests measured a baseline off the field -- throw a net, count its radius -- and started failing when ownership became live, because an earlier test in the same file still OWNED the talent that moves that figure. Module state persists across tests here by design, and the old rule made a leftover grant inert, so the pollution could not reach a figure and no baseline ever needed clearing. The rule change flipped every one of those leftovers live at once. Two things follow. A test that measures a base must OWN NOTHING first, explicitly, rather than relying on a rule elsewhere to make leftovers harmless. And when changing what makes state effective, the failures to expect are not in the code you touched: they are wherever shared state was being kept safe by the property you just removed.

The suite went from 19 s to 1280 s -- 67x -- right after a change to the render path, which reads exactly like a performance regression and sent me hunting one. There was none. A dev server was still running from a visual check and the game was open in the browser pane, driving requestAnimationFrame at 60 Hz on the same cores vitest was using. Closing the preview put the run back to 19 s with the code untouched. Two things follow. Stop the preview before timing anything, or the number measures your own browser tab. And when a slowdown appears with no plausible mechanism in the diff -- the change was in draw functions, which the node tests never call -- check what else is running before reading the code again.

Alex played the ranger and said the net was not stunning anything, including crows. Nine tests covered the net and all nine passed. The tests were right about the rule and blind to the ability: every one of them froze its target for the flight, and the helper that did it said why -- 'a passive crow drifts most of a radius in that time, so an unfrozen target turns every catch into a question about the drift'. That comment is the bug, noticed and written down as a reason to work around it. A net is aimed at a POINT and takes its whole flight to arrive, so the flight is a gap the target walks out of: at netSpeed 420 a full-draw throw was airborne 0.76 s while an aggro crow covered 305 px against a 70 px radius, doubled again by the late-wave escalation. It landed behind everything worth netting. Two things follow. When a test helper neutralises the thing a player would actually be doing -- freezing a chaser, parking a mover, pinning a spawn -- read the justification as a defect report and write the unfrozen case; the workaround marks the exact spot. And when a fixed-count wait passes only because some other figure happens to be slower, it is measuring the wrong thing: the HOLDFAST pin loop ran 60 frames and only reported a catch because the net used to take 17 of them, so speeding the net up made a caught body read as free. Stop the loop on the event, not on a count.

Three of four new Momentum tests failed on their first run, and all three failed the same way: they called setMomentum(0.6), then held a movement key for thirty frames, then asserted something about a meter at 0.6. But running is what FILLS that meter -- it is the entire mechanic -- so by frame two every one of them was measuring a full meter and the level they set was fiction. The failures were the honest kind (3 ghosts where fewer were expected, a sting already decayed to zero) and they read at first like bugs in the feature rather than in the test. The rule: when a test sets a piece of state and then drives the system, check whether the thing it is driving is the thing that WRITES that state. If it is, pin the value every frame instead of once at the top -- a hold parameter on the loop helper -- and say in the test why. The same shape catches anything sampled at an edge: momentumSting lasts 0.16 s, so a ten-frame run put the assertion past the flash it was checking for. Assert a flash on the frame it fires, not after a loop that outlives it.

The crossbow got a magazine of four volleys and a reload beat, and Alex played it and said the ranger 'can only have one shot of 3 arrows in flight instead of emptying the clip'. He was describing the feel exactly and the count was right the whole time: all four volleys left on CONSECUTIVE FRAMES -- 0, 1, 2, 3, which is 67 ms -- because the magazine had a size and a reload but no rate WITHIN it. Sixty-seven milliseconds is below what an eye separates, so a full clip read as one shot and the 1.1 s reload after it read as the weapon jamming. Four tests covered the magazine and not one noticed, because every one of them asked whether volleys came out and how many, never WHEN. Two rules. A resource with a capacity needs a rate as well, or the capacity is invisible: measure the frames a burst actually occupies before believing a count. And when a report describes a feel rather than a number ('it reads as one shot'), instrument the timing rather than re-checking the arithmetic -- the arithmetic was never wrong. The helper that emptied the magazine also had to stop pressing once per frame and start waiting for each volley's event, the same rule as every other fixed-count wait in this file.

'the ranger net > throws further, wider and longer' failed once in a full suite run, passed alone, and then passed in eleven consecutive full runs. Never caught in the act. The temptation is to shrug or to re-run until it happens; the useful move is to enumerate what COULD produce that exact failure and pin each one, so the next occurrence names its reason instead of starting the hunt again. Three candidates, and measuring them was worth more than the original hunt. The MAP was the obvious suspect -- the throw is 320 px due east down ten tiles of generated terrain -- and a 200-seed sweep pinning Math.random found zero bad maps, so terrain is exonerated and that is now a six-seed permanent guard. A leftover WIDE NET grant was live: the net's radius is lerp(min,max) + TALENTS.stat('wideNet') while every assertion compares against the raw CONFIG figure, and grants persist across tests in a file by design, so the helper now owns nothing first and a guard proves it. The AIM hazard was real but not yet reachable: rangerAt staged the hero with `p.aimAngle = 0` where CLAUDE.md says to use aimAt, and updatePlayer rewrites the angle from the pointer every step -- but throwNet releases the net before the sim has run once, so the staged angle survived and the first version of that guard passed with the fix removed. Adding ONE stepSim before the throw made it bite: the net flew -104 px instead of +320, backwards toward where the previous test had left the mouse. A guard that cannot fail is not a guard, and the way to find out is to revert the fix and watch -- which is the rule this repo already has, applied to a test's own staging rather than to the code under test.

Two different tests went red exactly once each during one session -- 'the ranger net > throws further, wider and longer' and 'the retinue holds the barrier gates > walks out of terrain it was pushed into' -- both only in a FULL run, both green alone and green in every full run afterwards. Neither was a game bug and neither was the map: they were seed-swept clean at 200 and 120 map seeds respectively, zero bad. The cause was vitest's default 5 s per-test timeout. The slowest tests in this suite run about 2 s on an idle machine -- a siege test that steps 240 frames, a net test that throws twice and waits for each to land -- and two and a half times headroom does not survive a developer's box doing anything else. This session had two background agents running their own vitest suites on the same cores the whole time. It is the same shape as preview-tab-skews-the-suite, where a browser preview drives rAF on those cores, and it presents completely differently from an assertion failure: the message is 'Test timed out in 5000ms', so grepping a log for AssertionError finds nothing and the failure looks like a mystery. testTimeout is 20 s now. Two rules. When a test fails once and will not reproduce, check whether the failure was a TIMEOUT before hunting logic -- the message is the diagnosis and it costs one line of the log. And a gate that goes falsely red teaches people to re-run it, which is exactly how a true red gets waved through.

SIEGE sat behind `hidden: true` with six lines of comment explaining that nothing drove the spawners, so a run 'lands on the bastion and stays empty with nothing to fight and no way to end'. Every word of that had stopped being true: startSiegeRun builds towers and guards, updateSiege spawns each wave and promotes on clear, and both arms of the frame loop call it. The mode was finished and shipped hidden. Nobody caught it because the suite agreed with the comment -- one test asserted `hidden` was true and another asserted the row was absent from the menu, so the two things guarding the player from an unfinished mode were guarding a finished one, and a green suite read as confirmation. Two rules. First: an audit that finds a comment explaining why something is disabled must go and read the code it describes before believing it; the comment is a claim with a date on it and no way to fail. Second, and this is the part that made it invisible: EVERY siege test in the file starts with setMode('siege'), the internal door, which cannot tell you whether the menu row a player presses reaches anything at all. When a feature has a front door and a back door, at least one test has to come in the front -- this one drives MENU_SHOWN's own row and plays ten waves to a win through it.

Starting the dev preview from a worktree served a DIFFERENT worktree's code. The launch config named port 5173 and the server came up on 8090 running `vite --port 8090 --strictPort`, a command this worktree's package.json does not contain: the preview tool had run `npm run dev` from a sibling checkout. Nothing said so. The page looked exactly right -- same game, same title -- and the first devHooks read came back missing every field the change had just added, which reads as a build that did not reload. It was the wrong build. Two things follow. Before trusting a preview, ask the page for something only your change has (`Object.keys(g.SOME_NEW_TABLE)`) rather than assuming the server is yours, and check the server log for the working directory it printed. And when a page is missing a change you just made, suspect the wrong SOURCE before the wrong cache -- several clones of this repo sit on disk.

`drawUltimateAura` paints BEFORE the body, deliberately -- it should read as something around the hero rather than stuck on him -- so every pixel it puts inside the silhouette is painted over by the sprite a moment later. Two of five new auras were drawn on the body and were therefore invisible in play: chevrons nine pixels wide on a twenty-four-wide knight showed only the one frame that cleared his boots, and falling shafts lost their middles to his chest. Both were correct code, both passed every test, and neither could be caught by reading them. The existing five all draw at a radius of 17 or more, or on the floor -- that was not decoration, it was the constraint, and nothing had written it down. Draw a body aura outside the silhouette, and check a new one by rendering the hero with it ready beside the same hero with it on cooldown: the only difference on screen is the thing you drew.

EARTHSHATTER's ready aura is cracks radiating on the floor, and the floor is drawn at GROUND_SQUASH, so every ray shallower than about forty degrees lands in the same two rows. Six of them from a common centre came out as one solid orange slab under his boots -- a puddle, not a floor coming apart -- and nothing in the code said so: each ray was correct on its own and the test only checked that something was drawn. Two things follow. On a squashed plane, radial marks need diagonal headings, an empty middle and lengths that are not mirror images of each other, or they merge. And a ring several things travel round may pass BEHIND the hero, because the ones in front go on saying what it is, while a ring with ONE thing on it may not: THE BIG ONE's single spark simply went out for a quarter of its lap, which is the beat that ability is made of. Two ring rows, and the rule for which is which.

Two auras shipped painted under the hero, and the fix that round was to move those two shapes. Redrawing all ten made the same mistake available ten more times, so the rule moved into the one function every painter writes a block through: it refuses any cell the sprite covers. That turns 'remember the silhouette' into something you cannot forget, and it pays twice -- shapes that straddle him are now drawn WHOLE and come out occluded, which is what standing in a ring is supposed to look like, where hand-avoiding the body had produced shapes with holes in them. The test is the same rule read off the finished grid, so it fails by ability and frame rather than by a screenshot nobody takes.

The ten ready auras moved from a 4px grid to a 1px one, and the figure that made the decision safe was AREA, not cell count. One ring is 48 cells at 4px and 724 at 1px -- thirteen times the cells and the same ink, 768 canvas pixels against 724 -- so a finer grain buys shape and costs nothing, PROVIDED a mark that was one 4px cell is drawn three cells wide rather than one. Drawn one wide it would have been a different picture: a ready tell is read across a field at a glance, the canvas is scaled DOWN to fit a small viewport and never up, and the scanline overlay darkens one screen row in four. So when a grid gets finer, hold the ink and spend the grain on the places that were approximations -- here rings that were octagons, cracks that were straight rays, and a swept beam whose sweep was not drawn.

Four defects in the auras survived the 4px grid and were obvious at 1px, all of them present before the change and none catchable by a test. THE LEAP put two chevrons two rungs apart on a four-rung ladder, so frames 0 and 2 held the same pair of rows and so did 1 and 3: a two-frame flicker paying for four cache entries -- evenly spaced travellers on an N-step cycle give N/gcd(step,N) distinct pictures, so make the spacing coprime with the step count. THE BIG ONE's ring row was chosen so the spark clears the boots at every step and the BURN behind it, which reaches a fifth of a lap further round, did not: the head was cut off from its own trail. HARPOON's two bars each covered less arc than the hero's body hides, so one frame in four had both behind him. VORTEX was eight dots on a flat ellipse, which says ring, when the ability says inward. A coarse grid does not make these right, it makes them too blurry to see.

Proving a guard is load-bearing means deleting its line, running the test, and putting the line back -- and a script that does that in a loop over several guards is holding the only copy of uncommitted work. Mine crashed between the write and the restore (subprocess with text=True decoding vitest's output as cp1252 and dying on a box-drawing byte) and left `ultimate-aura.ts` on disk WITHOUT its occlusion guard. Nothing in git to fall back on, because the whole redraw was uncommitted, and the file still typechecked and still passed most of the suite, so it would have been committed silently. Two rules: restore in a `finally`, and take a copy on disk first. Under the Bash tool also pass capture_output without text=True and decode with errors='replace' -- vitest prints characters cp1252 has no mapping for.

A one-cell mark on the aura grid is not a finer version of a mark, it is a mark that is gone. The canvas is scaled DOWN to fit any viewport under 1760x1104 and never up, so a fractional factor deletes whole pixel rows outright, and the scanline overlay darkens one row in four on top of that: the hairline comes out as dashes in places that differ per viewport. Four shipped in the first cut of the 1px redraw -- VORTEX's inbound tracks, CARPET BOMB's fuse and the two arms of its spark -- each with a comment defending the choice, because at grid scale they look correct and the loss only happens on the way to the screen. The floor belongs in the BRUSH, not in review: `dot` is the one chokepoint `seg` and `arc` both route through, and it now throws below THIN, the way `blk` refuses to paint into the body. Every aura is already built by the suite at every frame, so the guard needed no test of its own.

Three commander tests broke on a change to a pace preset they never mention. `runToWave` stepped one escalation interval per wave and read that interval out of CONFIG, so it looked pace-proof; what it actually depended on was how long the field stayed busy. Stretching the interval from 4.5 s to 8 s did two things at once: it gave the garrison longer to work on an idle hero, who died, and it gave `openChooserWhenClear` a lull long enough to open a queued pick -- and a run parked on a ceremony screen never advances a wave, so the commander never arrived and `go('boss_fight')` threw on an illegal transition out of 'chooser'. Reading a figure from CONFIG is not the same as being independent of it. A climb in this repo needs three things, not one: heal on a cadence rather than once a wave, dismiss whatever ceremony a lull opens, and stop on the event rather than on a frame count.

Asked to tune the game down, I cut crow density across the easier rungs and the answer came back: the crows were never the problem, and thinning them made the easy rungs boring rather than kinder. What made the game unwinnable was the chase. whiteCrowAggroSpeed is 300 against a roster whose quickest hero runs 250 and whose slowest runs 150, and waveCrowAggroMult doubled it by wave 22, so no character and no upgrade has ever been able to break away from a white crow. Worse, three of the four figures that decide a chase -- crowAggroSpeed, whiteCrowPassiveSpeed, whiteCrowAggroSpeed -- sat directly under a CONFIG comment saying the pace preset owned them and were in no preset at all, so every difficulty the game had ran the same chase. Two rules out of it. A difficulty knob is the one the player loses to, not the one that is easiest to turn: instrument what actually kills the run before picking it. And a comment claiming a group of figures is owned somewhere is worth checking against the code, because the ones that were missing were exactly the ones nobody had thought about.
